causalModel.founding: A gang that works the channel must sleep on land. The gang's families follow it to the camp. The camp is forty years old.
causalModel.siteAdvantages: The camp stands on a slope of firm ground above the marsh. The slope lies below the Border road. The top terrace stays dry enough for a hatching shed.
causalModel.occupantsMotive: The families belong to people on the gang's roll. They live within walking distance of the roll's work.
causalModel.pressures: The camp has no claim on the Hist a day upriver. The families stay because the clutch is in the shed.
causalModel.wouldChangeIf: If the clutch is lost, the families leave the camp. They go to places that the ledger does not record.

districts.notes: Terraces of levelled earth cut into the slope between the Border road and the marsh, one shelter on each.

why.what: The camp is the gang's living quarter. It holds two sleeping sheds, two family tents, the overseers' hut and the hatching shed.
why.whyHere: The camp stands on firm ground within a walk of the barge. It lies below the Border road.
why.whySpot: The slope faces north over the marsh. The Border road runs along the top of the slope.
why.whyNeighbours: Alten Corimont lies across the water to the north.
why.playerPurpose: The gang's families live in the camp. The clutch is kept in the camp too.
why.microGeography: The slope is steep and cut into terraces. Each terrace is a few paces wide.

districts.notes: The work yard on the bluff edge, the stair down its face and the landing on the shallows below, with the barge's berth beside it.

why.what: The district holds the gang's work yard, the stair down the bluff and the landing. The barge lies at the landing.
why.whyHere: The bluff drops straight to the only water near the camp that is deep enough to float a loaded boat.
why.whySpot: The district lies below the west sleeping shed. The bluff edge there is flat enough to stack timber.
why.whyNeighbours: The terraces of the camp rise behind the district to the south. The marsh channel lies in front of it.
why.playerPurpose: The gang stacks its work in the yard and hauls it down to the barge. The district is the way between the camp and the water.
why.microGeography: The district is a flat strip of ground on the bluff edge. It stands over a nine-metre drop. A mud shelf lies under shallow water below the drop.

parcels.orientationWhy: The hatching shed's door faces north-west. From the door the terraces fall away to the camp's fire.

why.what: The hatching shed is a bamboo hut on stilt legs. It is kept warmer and cleaner than the sleeping sheds.
why.whyHere: The clutch has to be kept dry and warm. The hatching shed stands on the highest terrace.
why.whySpot: The hatching shed stands on the top terrace. It lies beside the Border road, furthest from the water.
why.whyNeighbours: The family tents and the cookfire are on the terrace below.
why.playerPurpose: The clutch-keeper keeps the camp's eggs in the hatching shed.
why.microGeography: The terrace is levelled and made of packed earth. Two lanterns hang at the door. A totem stands beside the door.

playerPurpose.note: The camp's egg clutch is kept here.

parcels.orientationWhy: The overseers' hut door faces east onto the yard way. The door is in sight of the fire and the sheds.

why.what: The overseers' hut is a bamboo hut on stilt legs. It houses the camp's two overseers.
why.whyHere: The brokers keep their overseers among the families.
why.whySpot: The hut stands on the middle terrace. It lies between the sleeping sheds and the tents.
why.whyNeighbours: The cookfire is a few paces east of the hut. The sleeping sheds are below the hut.
why.playerPurpose: The camp's overseers sleep in the hut. The overseers keep their accounts there.
why.microGeography: The terrace is levelled. The yard way runs past the hut door.

playerPurpose.note: The broker's overseers live among the families whom they watch.
On the night of the raid, the player chooses a witness at this door.

parcels.orientationWhy: The west sleeping shed has an open front facing south-east. The front opens onto the yard way.

why.what: The west sleeping shed is a thatched half pavilion on log posts. Its front is open. Most of the families sleep there.
why.whyHere: The families sleep under open thatch on the lowest terrace. The root path climbs down to the reeds beside the terrace.
why.whySpot: The west sleeping shed stands on the lowest terrace, nearest the water.
why.whyNeighbours: The second sleeping shed stands beside it to the east.
why.playerPurpose: Most of the gang's families sleep in the west shed at night.
why.microGeography: The floor is packed earth under thatch. Nets dry at the corner.

playerPurpose.note: The root climb up the west bank starts behind this shed.

parcels.orientationWhy: The east sleeping shed has an open front facing south. The front looks up the yard way.

why.what: The east sleeping shed is the second thatched half pavilion. The families' cooking things stand in front of it.
why.whyHere: The shed stands below the cookfire. The families who cook sleep closest to the fire.
why.whySpot: The east sleeping shed stands on the lowest terrace, at the foot of the yard way.
why.whyNeighbours: The first sleeping shed is beside it to the west. The cookfire is above it.
why.playerPurpose: The gang's families sleep and cook at the east shed.
why.microGeography: The floor is packed earth under thatch. A cooking pot and stores stand in front.

playerPurpose.note: The opening night begins here, with the families at the fire.

parcels.orientationWhy: The east family tent has an open front facing west. The front opens onto the yard.

why.what: The east family tent is hide over poles. It stands on its own small terrace below the road.
why.whyHere: The camp is forty years old. The families still live in tents and sheds.
why.whySpot: The east family tent stands on the east terrace, below the Border road.
why.whyNeighbours: The hatching shed is above the tent. The cookfire is below it.
why.playerPurpose: One of the gang's families lives in the tent. Its baskets stand at the door.
why.microGeography: The terrace is small and levelled. Baskets stand at the front.

parcels.orientationWhy: The south family tent has an open front facing north-east. The front opens onto the yard way.

why.what: The south family tent is hide over poles. It stands a few paces from the hatching shed.
why.whyHere: The clutch-keeper's family pitched beside the shed. A family member is always near the eggs.
why.whySpot: The south family tent stands on the south terrace, beside the hatching shed.
why.whyNeighbours: The hatching shed is a few paces to the east.
why.playerPurpose: The clutch-keeper's family lives in the tent. The tent is close to the eggs in the shed.
why.microGeography: The terrace is small and levelled. It lies beside the yard way.

parcels.orientationWhy: A path cut into banked earth falls west along the bluff face from the lip to a bench in the corner. The timber stair turns back east from the bench and runs down the foot of the bluff to the shelf.

why.what: The way down is a switchback. A path is cut into earth banked against the bluff. A timber stair of two flights runs below it.
why.whyHere: The bluff drops about ten metres from the work yard to the mud shelf. It is too steep to walk straight down.
why.whySpot: The cut starts at the lip below the work yard. It turns on a bench of earth in the corner under the west sleeping shed.
why.whyNeighbours: The landing dock starts two metres from the foot of the stair, on the dry shelf.
why.playerPurpose: The cut and the stair are the way from the camp down to the landing and the barge.
why.microGeography: The head is a level shelf on the lip, 10.25 m above the mud shelf, with a lit fire-bowl and two poles. The bench at the turn is 6.5 m up. The stair's foot stands on the dry mud shelf.

parcels.orientationWhy: The landing dock runs north from the foot of the stair. It crosses the shallows to the deep water where the barge lies.

why.what: The landing dock is two plank spans on piles. It runs from the foot of the stair out over the shallows.
why.whyHere: The shelf below the bluff is too shallow for the barge. The barge lies in the deeper water to the north.
why.whySpot: The dock stands at the foot of the stair. It runs straight out to the first water a metre deep.
why.whyNeighbours: The stair climbs from the dock's south end. The rowboat is tied off the dock's north end.
why.playerPurpose: The stair meets the water at the dock. The rowboat is moored at the dock.
why.microGeography: The dock's piles stand in silt. The water is half a metre deep at the shore end and a metre deep at the far end.

parcels.orientationWhy: The barge lies bow west along the channel. Its open waist faces the strand so that the pier meets it.

why.what: The barge is a Breton hull with its masts and rigging gone. The gang keeps it as a floating work deck. It has a lean-to in the waist, a crane on the bow and stripped planks on the stern.
why.whyHere: The camp breaks salvage for planking. The hull is the camp's store. The gang is counted aboard the hull.
why.whySpot: The barge lies in the channel east of the landing. The water is a metre deep along its whole length.
why.whyNeighbours: The barge pier runs from the barge's waist to the strand. The landing and the stair lie off the barge's bow.
why.playerPurpose: The overseers process the gang on the barge and read the roll there. The opening fight breaks out on the barge's deck.
why.microGeography: The barge's keel rests in the silt of a channel a metre deep. A dry mud bank lies to the north. The strand under the bluff lies to the south.

parcels.orientationWhy: The barge pier runs north from the strand to the barge's waist. Its steps are at the shore end.

why.what: The barge pier is a plank dock at deck height on piles. It has steps down to the strand and a plank across to the barge.
why.whyHere: The barge's deck stands two metres over the water. Loads and prisoners go aboard level from a high pier.
why.whySpot: The pier runs straight out from the flat strand to the middle of the barge's waist.
why.whyNeighbours: The barge lies at the pier's far end. The landing and the stair are a short wade west along the strand.
why.playerPurpose: The pier is the way between the strand and the barge's deck. The gang and the visitor both use it.
why.microGeography: The pier's steps come down onto a raised pad of trodden mud at the foot of the bluff. Its piles stand in a metre of water at the far end.

routes.why: The way runs in from the Border road to the door of the hatching shed.
The camp's main way runs down the terraces from the hatching shed to the sleeping sheds.
A short spur leaves the yard way for the overseers' door.
A spur crosses the lowest terrace to the west sleeping shed.
A spur leaves the yard way and crosses to the east family tent.
A spur leaves the yard way for the south family tent's mouth.
The way runs from the front of the west sleeping shed to the head of the stairs. The stairs go down the bluff to the landing.
The way runs along the strand from the foot of the stairs to the barge pier.
The way is the end of the gang's walk from the barge. It joins the Border road above the camp.
The cut earth of the way down continues to the head of the plank landing and meets the planks there.

landmarks.notes: The camp's one fire, on its own levelled patch of the middle terrace.

why.what: The camp's cooking fire is ringed with stones. A pot, an urn and a bench stand beside it.
why.whyHere: The families cook and sit together after a shift. The overseers keep the fire in view.
why.whySpot: The fire stands on the middle terrace between the overseers' hut and the east tent. The ground there is levelled for the fire.
why.whyNeighbours: The overseers' door faces the fire. The east sleeping shed is below it.
why.playerPurpose: The fire is the heart of the camp at night. The opening scene gathers the gang there.
why.microGeography: The fire stands on a small level patch cut into the slope of the middle terrace.

landmarks.notes: The gang's cut timber stacked at the head of the stair, waiting to be hauled down to the barge.

why.what: A long stack of cut timber stands in the work yard. A cart, a chopping block and sacks stand beside it.
why.whyHere: The gang owes labour to the yard. The gang cuts timber. The timber work pays the debt down.
why.whySpot: The timber stack stands on flat ground at the bluff edge. It stands beside the head of the stair to the landing.
why.whyNeighbours: The west sleeping shed stands above the timber stack. The stair down to the barge starts beside the stack.
why.playerPurpose: The timber stack shows the gang's forced labour. It stands in view before the barge is reached.
why.microGeography: The stack stands on a levelled strip on the lip of the bluff.

landmarks.notes: A large firewood pile with a small one beside it, on the mud shelf at the land end of the landing dock.

why.what: A large pile of cut firewood lies on the mud shelf next to the landing dock. A small pile of firewood lies beside the large pile.
why.whyHere: The gang carries the yard's timber down the stair. The gang loads the barge from this end of the dock.
why.whySpot: The piles stand on the dry shelf between the foot of the stair and the end of the dock.
why.whyNeighbours: The stair comes down beside the piles. The dock runs out from the piles to the barge.
why.playerPurpose: The piles show where the gang's work ends up. The gang's work ends up on the barge.
why.microGeography: The piles stand on a levelled patch of the mud shelf at the water's edge. The patch lies under the bluff.

questSockets.why: The camp's fire burns on the middle terrace. The families sit at the fire on the night of the raid.
The door of the hatching shed is a quest point. The clutch-keeper comes out of the door on the night of the raid.
The yard way runs between the overseers' door and the tents.
The dead clutch lies inside the hatching shed. The hatching shed stands on the top terrace.
The hatching shed's door is where the clutch is kept.
The epilogue shows the yard again to establish whether the families stayed.
The steep bank lies below the west sleeping shed. The bank is the climb down to the reeds.
A sleeping place lies under the west shed's thatch.

approaches.sequence: The gang's walk from the barge comes up onto the Border road. The walk joins the road east of the camp. The camp's roofs lie below the road to the west.
approaches.wayfinding: The road runs west, down to the hatching shed.

networkTerminals.why: The gang's walk from the barge ends beside the Border road.

combatSpaces.why: The terraces are narrow and lie on a steep slope. Drops lie between the terraces.

scaleGrounding.loreSource: catalogue record Gang Ground (muster yard, M2); world/sources/lore/topics/labour-and-bondage.md (the Owing)
scaleGrounding.why: Four families of the gang live in the camp. The clutch-keeper and two overseers also live there. The rest of the gang sleeps on the barge.

candidates.why: The plotted anchor's own slope has a gentler western side. The western side lies between the Border road and the marsh. Levelled terraces on the western side hold every shelter.
The plotted anchor point lies at the eastern end of the slope.
candidates.rejectedBecause: The anchor point itself stands on a 16 degree slope. The anchor point stands 21 m above the water.
